stemMd: Experiment 2 differed from Experiment 1 in only one respect: the extract was held at $80^{\circ}\text{C}$ for 10 minutes and cooled back to $25^{\circ}\text{C}$ before use. What was the most likely purpose of Experiment 2?

options.label: A
options.textMd: To increase the volume of oxygen that could be collected in 60 s.

options.label: B
options.textMd: To find the pH at which the extract releases the most oxygen.

options.label: C
options.textMd: To test whether hydrogen peroxide breaks down more quickly at higher reaction temperatures.

options.label: D
options.textMd: To test whether a heat-sensitive substance in the extract was responsible for the release of oxygen.

explanationMd:
Work out what the single change could possibly reveal. The one thing the student altered was the *history* of the extract: it was cooked and then cooled. Everything else — the 5.0 mL of extract, the 20.0 mL of 3% hydrogen peroxide, the buffers, the 60 s collection time and the $25^{\circ}\text{C}$ **reaction** temperature — was identical.

So the comparison answers one question: does it matter whether the extract has been heated? Table 3 answers it emphatically. At every pH the heated extract released 2 mL or less, against 6 to 31 mL for the unheated extract. Something in the extract is doing the work, and heating destroys it — which is what "heat-sensitive substance" means.

Check the logic by noting the detail that rules out the temperature explanation: the extract was **cooled back to $25^{\circ}\text{C}$** before it was added. Both experiments ran their reactions at the same temperature, so no difference in the results can be attributed to the reaction being hotter or colder. That one clause in the procedure is deliberately load-bearing — in an experiment-comparison question, the phrase that restores a variable to its original value is usually the phrase that decides the answer.

distractorRationale.c: Misses the cooling step. Because the heated extract was returned to $25^{\circ}\text{C}$ before it was added, both experiments ran at the same reaction temperature, so nothing in this design compares reaction temperatures at all.
distractorRationale.b: Describes what Experiment 1 already did. The five pH values were tested in Experiment 1, and repeating them with damaged extract adds nothing to the search for an optimum — the heated column is nearly flat at 1 to 2 mL.
distractorRationale.a: States the opposite of what happened. Heating reduced oxygen release from a range of 6-31 mL down to 2 mL or less, and no scientist repeating a trial with a deliberately damaged sample is trying to increase the yield.

accessibilityText: The question compares Experiment 1, in which unheated extract released 6, 18, 31, 24 and 9 millilitres of oxygen at pH 4 through 8, with Experiment 2, in which extract first held at 80 degrees Celsius for 10 minutes and then cooled back to 25 degrees released 1, 1, 2, 1 and 1 millilitres at the same pH values. Both experiments ran their reactions at 25 degrees Celsius.

independentSolve.workingNotes: The only changed variable is prior heating of the extract, and the reaction itself was still run at 25 C, so Experiment 2 isolates whether heat destroys an active (heat-sensitive) component; the near-zero volumes (1-2 mL) confirm that framing. (a) is contradicted by the data, (b) describes Experiment 1's pH variable, and (c) is ruled out because the reaction temperature was identical in both experiments.

review.notes: Author solved the item and attempted to defend each distractor before keying it. The stimulus states explicitly that the heated extract was cooled back to 25 C and that both experiments therefore ran at the same reaction temperature, which closes off the only otherwise-defensible alternative.
